AI security · Field report · Second edition, update 20

October 3, 2026

Grading the Grader

A security scanner built for AI-generated apps spent September trying to prove that it does not cry wolf. On October 1 it learned to say what it could not see and to show how it found each thing, and Carlos ran it on a real site. A pull request opened at 23:29 UTC that day addressed three gaps the report screens showed, and it was merged on Carlos’s word at 11:23 UTC on October 2. This second edition puts every test, scan and artifact in one place, with what each proves and what it leaves open.

The short version

What the evidence supports after the fix session

SecScan is an outside-in security scanner. Give it a web address and it reads the public site, checks the domain’s DNS and mail records, tests a list of known weak spots and returns a grade from A to F, with fixes written for the stack it found. It was built for people who ship apps faster than they can audit them, and for the AI tools that generate those apps.

Finding problems is the easy half. The hard half is leaving out problems that are not there. A scanner that cries wolf teaches its readers to ignore it. A scanner that stays quiet looks the same as one that is broken. Since September 7 the project has been trying to tell those two apart, using planted flaws, blind judges, live sweeps of well-run websites and hand checks of nearly everything the scanner said.

On October 1 it added a tool that matters as much, which is showing the work. A report now says what ran and what was skipped, how each finding was found, and when the scan never saw the app at all. The first report from a real site after those fixes, a scan of seclayer.app that Carlos supplied, shows the ledger working in production: 33 of 44 tests ran, 11 were skipped, and each skipped test gives its reason. Reported The next section is about that, and the one after it covers the fixes that came from scans of live apps in which the scanner was reading something other than the app. A pull request opened late on October 1 addressed three gaps that the report screens showed, and it was merged on Carlos’s word on October 2. It has a subsection of its own.

The three asks, scored

On October 1 Carlos asked for three things: scans that reach the real app, transparency, and every fix taken care of. Each row says what is done, what is only shown on stand-ins, and what nobody has checked. The short answer is still not yet. The fixes of the fix session are merged, a pull request that adds three more has merged too, and the proof is not in, because most of it needs scans of live apps and the sessions that worked on this had no outbound access.

How to read the marks

Verified means I recomputed it from raw output files, or read it in the repository, the shared project folder or the GitHub Actions record, on October 1 or 2. Reran means I ran it myself on October 1 or 2: the scanner built from master after PR 14, after PR 15 or after PR 16, the fixture gate and the test suites, against local stand-in apps and clean hosts, the report screens of master after PR 16 in a browser with the API stubbed, and the same screens, the tests and a rescan of the fixture from the branch of draft PR 17. Nothing I reran touched a real site. Reported means a repository document, a commit message or something Carlos supplied states it, and I did not rerun it. Researched means it comes from the Sept 24 competitor research, which was spot-checked on Sept 28 for three rivals and not re-checked since. Inference means I reasoned it from what I read and did not observe it. A number with no mark is arithmetic on marked numbers, or a definition.

Names for the code. In the October 1 sections, “master” alone means the master of the first edition, 5d19cad, before the fix session. “The merged code” and “merged master” mean master as it was before PR 17 merged, 28ad16d. “Draft PR 17” and “the branch” mean its head when I ran it, a8d3a03 and later dada93e. The merge into master is 06f61f1, and I have run nothing on it.

The field

The pitch is already on sale, and cheaper

Researched The research behind this section was done on September 24 and spot-checked on September 28 for the three closest rivals, CheckVibe, Vibe App Scanner and StackHawk. Nothing material moved in those four days. The rest of the field was not re-researched, and nobody ran a competitor’s scanner. Prices are as reported on the day and change often.

The pitch has buyers and rivals

Vibe App Scanner, CheckVibe and VibeEval scan a live URL for apps built on Lovable, Bolt or Supabase, hand back a paste-into-your-editor fix and ship an MCP server. They charge $19 to $49 a month for 20 to 250 scans. SecScan’s pitch, an outside view of an AI-built app with a fix you can paste, is the same pitch.

Even the leader looks small

Vibe App Scanner reportedly averages about $500 a month in revenue after six months. That figure is self-reported and unverified. The category holds more than 25 look-alike scanners, several already dead. The research’s advice was to plan for slow money.

Builders give away a baseline

Lovable runs a free scan on every publish and sells a $100 live-app pentest, refunded if nothing is found. Bolt, Base44, Replit and Supabase bundle checks as well. SecScan looks from outside, on any platform, continuously. That gap is real. It is narrower than “nobody checks these apps.”

Depth is not the pitch

Invicti, Burp and Detectify have years more depth. The Sept 24 research held that ZAP and Nuclei, which are free, match or beat SecScan on headers and TLS in general. On the project’s own vulnerable app SecScan beat both by a wide margin, headers included (13 of 13 against ZAP’s 10 and Nuclei’s 2). That app is SecScan’s own checklist made executable, so the result shows coverage of the list. It does not show superiority.

An MCP server is table stakes now

Detectify, StackHawk, Pentest-Tools, PortSwigger, Bright, ProjectDiscovery, CheckVibe and Vibe App Scanner all have one. StackHawk has shipped a GitHub Action with SARIF upload for years at $39 per contributor per month. SecScan now has an MCP server with OAuth 2.1, a REST API, a CLI, a GitHub Action and SARIF export. That is parity. The Action’s own repository is not published yet.

What no rival was seen advertising

A fail-closed, ownership-verified gate before any active test. A per-scan ledger of what ran, what was skipped and why. An AI held to the scanner’s findings, with a switch that keeps findings away from the AI provider entirely. Compliance mapping that never claims a pass. A deliberately vulnerable test app the scanner is checked against. Competitors may do some of this quietly. It is also invisible to a buyer until someone shows it. Carlos believes this kind of transparency will go a long way, and the section on showing the work sets out what it covers today.

The product

What SecScan is, and what it says it is not

How a scan runs

The passive stage reads the public response: headers, cookies, HTML, JavaScript, DNS and mail records, certificates. The probe stage asks for well-known paths and endpoints, such as exposed files, source maps, API specs, GraphQL and Supabase or Firebase configuration, and a crawler follows up to 20 internal pages. The active stage sends test inputs, including injection payloads and API calls with and without credentials. It runs only against a domain whose owner has been verified.

When ownership is not verified, the active stage is skipped and the report says so. The sentence “Active security testing was skipped for this scan” appears on all 22 graded sites in the Sept 24 sweep. Verified

Every scan writes a ledger. Each test is recorded as ran, skipped with a reason, or failed, so a crashed probe family shows up instead of passing for a clean result. Since October 1 a test with nothing to look at is recorded as skipped, with its reason, and no longer as “ran, 0 findings.” A scan that never reaches the app, because a challenge or a platform page answered, is withheld and gets no grade, and since PR 15 its test list marks every test that read that page as “not tested on the app.” A real scan of a domain lists 44 tests: the 40 that the scan itself records and four from the worker, the SSL Labs grade, DNS records, subdomain enumeration and a port scan. Showing the work covers all of it.

How grades work

The risk score adds severity weights and caps at 100: critical 30, high 15, medium 5, low 1, info 0. Grades follow the score. A is 10 or less, B is 25 or less, C is 45 or less, D is 65 or less, and F is anything above. Info findings carry no weight on purpose, so a site with a dozen presentation notes can still grade A. Higher scores are worse. A scan that never saw the app has no score and no grade, and the page says “Coverage incomplete.” Verified The Sept 24 table reproduces exactly from the raw output using these weights.

How many checks

Three numbers circulate, and they count different things. The check catalog, whose total is derived from its entries and enforced by a test, holds 144 checks. It held 143 after PR 14, 140 on September 26 and 129 on September 24. The generated finding index lists 315 distinct finding names across 60 modules and 38 categories (85 critical, 73 high, 55 medium, 32 low, 70 info), because one piece of detection logic can emit many named findings. It listed 314 after PR 14 and 310 on September 30. The README said 115 and now says 144. PR 16 added the one new check, the note that says why a TLS grade is below A. Verified My own run of the check index on master now agrees. Reran

The catalog test records the move from 140 to 143 as itemising GitHub source-code secret scanning, LLM prompt-injection extraction and the active race-condition probe. PR 16 moved it from 143 to 144 for the TLS grade note.

What it ships with

  • A web app, a REST API at /api/v1 with an OpenAPI document and SARIF export, and a CLI with a GitHub Action (the Action’s repository is not yet published).
  • An MCP server with OAuth 2.1, discovery, dynamic registration, PKCE and rotating refresh tokens.
  • Monitoring of up to 3 or 5 sites, a free “fixed this? check it” re-test (10 a day), a “what changed since your last scan” card, and a curl reproduction line for findings that can be replayed.
  • Fix prompts written for the detected platform, now covering nine hosting platforms, and an AI analysis that can be switched off per account so findings never reach the AI provider.
  • A report that shows its work: a ledger of every test, “How this was found” on each finding, and a “Withheld from this report” list.
  • Compliance mapping to ASVS, SOC 2, PCI, ISO 27001, NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 and the HIPAA technical safeguards. It never claims a pass.

Where it runs

A Node API server with a pg-boss job queue, PostgreSQL 16 and headless Chromium for rendering single-page apps. The repository builds two Docker images, web and secscan, and production is described as Railway services at secscan.us. A Docker Compose guide covers any Linux host. Reported

What it does not do

  • It does not test business logic, and broken access control needs two logins or is skipped.
  • It is an automated scanner. It is not a penetration test and never claims to be one.
  • No outside party has reproduced its test results. It has no customers, reviews or certifications to point to yet, and one person is behind it.
  • Its name is generic, and other companies use it. The product now brands as “SecScan.us,” while the repository and web app are named VibeScan.

The headline · new in this edition

A scanner that shows its work

Carlos’s view, stated on October 1, is that transparency is the one thing SecScan has that no other scanner or company has, and that it will go a long way. This section was written while PR 17 was a draft. Master in it means 28ad16d, before the merge at 11:23 UTC on October 2, and the draft is PR 17. It sets out what a report from that master shows its reader, how I know, what the first report from a real site looked like, what the screens look like, what pull request 17 changes on those screens, and where the showing stops.

Many of the defects in the accuracy ledger (66 rows, in Appendix A) share a shape. A report described something other than the app, or said it had checked something it never looked at, and nothing on the page let the reader tell. The project’s answer on October 1 was to put the evidence on the page: what was tested, what was skipped and why, how each finding was found, and what the scan refused to report.

This is an incomplete result, not a clean one.

The scanner’s own note when it reaches a sign-in page instead of the app. Raw output of the merged code on a Vercel Deployment Protection stand-in.

What the report can claim, and what it cannot

Researched The September 24 research found no rival advertising a per-scan ledger of what ran, what was skipped and why. That was vendor pages read on one day and spot-checked on September 28 for three rivals. Nobody compared what a rival’s report contains, so “no other scanner does this” is a hypothesis. “Every SecScan report shows its work” is a claim the code supports, and the rest of this section is the evidence for it. The competitive context is in A crowded field.

When a scan never saw the app, the test list now says so

Withholding the findings is half of being honest about a scan that a sign-in wall, a platform page or a bot challenge answered. The other half is the coverage list. After PR 14 that list still showed most of its tests as “ran,” so a reader of the coverage card could take it for “checked, and clean.” The fix session opened PR 15 at 10:03 UTC to change that, and Carlos merged it at 10:38 UTC as 4e291bc. It is one commit, six files, 76 lines added and 4 removed. I built its head before it merged and scanned the stand-ins again. The merged tree is identical to that head. Reran Verified The tree comparison, with git.

The rule is a short list. DNS and email authentication, mail transport security, subdomain takeover and GitHub source code secrets never read the page that answered, so they keep their result. Every other test that ran becomes “skipped” with the reason “not tested on the app,” its finding count goes to zero and its list of names is deleted. A test added later starts as “not tested” on a withheld scan until someone adds it to the list, so the default is to say less. Verified In the diff of scannerCoverage.ts.

The change is the same wherever the answering page came from, and it touches no other scan. The reason names what answered: “a sign-in page answered instead of the app,” “the hosting platform answered instead of the app” or “a bot-protection page answered instead of the site.” The challenge stand-in is one I wrote for this edition. It serves the fingerprints that the scanner documents for a Cloudflare challenge, so it shows that the branch works. It does not show what a real challenge looks like. Reran

The report screens, seen on stand-ins

Until this edition, what this section says a report shows rested on code, raw output and one PDF. I had not looked at the screens. I have now. The frontend of master after PR 16 ran in Chromium on its development server, with the API stubbed inside the browser. The stubbed responses were built from the saved output of my own scans, by the worker’s report builder and the route’s response schema, so the page received the shapes that production sends. No API server, login or database was involved, and nothing touched a real site. The scans are three of the stand-ins used above: the Vercel sign-in wall scanned passively, the vulnerable fixture scanned as its owner, and the hardened app. Reran

The screen does what the code says. The cover carries no score. The coverage card counts 3 of 42 tests as run, 37 as skipped and 2 as failed. The withheld card lists all 12 findings under the name of the platform that answered, each with its reason. Of the 42 rows, 40 are the scanner’s and two are the worker’s side rows, one for the SSL Labs grade and one for reconnaissance. Both failed, because both need the network. When they succeed the worker records four rows, which is why Carlos’s real scan lists 44. The last crop in Figure 3 is the list under those cards, and the third bullet below picks it up. On the scan that reached the app, the same card shows 33 of 42 tests run. Its 7 skipped tests give reasons about the app, such as no Supabase project in the page, where the wall scan’s reasons are about the scan: a sign-in page answered, or the domain was not verified. The OWASP card shows PR 16’s first fix on a screen. Two Info notes under Security Misconfiguration are drawn in grey and do not count as flagged, while a Critical and a Low finding do. Reran

The four panels are the four kinds the code can produce, and each reads as the code says. A finding the scanner read from the page names its check and says no attack traffic was involved. A finding from an active test names its check and says test requests were sent. A finding with no check on record shows a fallback line and still lists its request. A scan note carries the line “A note about the scan itself, not a finding about your site.” Both notes on the sign-in wall scan show it, because the code gives it to every item in the Scan Coverage category. Draft PR 17 lifts the limit to 500, and a rescan of the fixture from its branch names the check for all 199 findings. Reran
  • An active-test panel can list no requests. The panel for the XSS finding names its check and says the scanner sent test requests, and then lists none. It lists only evidence lines that start with a method and an address, such as GET /path, and this finding’s evidence is written as “Endpoint: /search?q=<payload>.” The panel is accurate. For an active test it names the check and does not show the requests, which are the part a reader would want to repeat. Reran Verified The pattern, in provenance.ts. Draft PR 17 reads both shapes. On a rescan of the fixture from its branch, 2 of the 24 findings from active tests list no request, down from 8 on master, and the panel says so for those two. Reran
  • On a withheld scan, four surfaces list the scan’s own notes as confirmed findings. On the sign-in wall scan the owner’s page heads the section Identified Vulnerabilities with a count of 2. A green bar reads “2 confirmed” with “100% high-confidence” at its right, and a second bar headed “Confirmed findings” says the two are high confidence and tells the owner to “act on these” (the last crop in Figure 3). The share page, the print layout and the Markdown copy also put the two items under “Confirmed findings.” Only the PDF export calls them “Findings (2).” The items are the scan’s own Info notes, active testing was skipped and a sign-in page answered, and each says when opened that it is a note about the scan (Figure 5). The page splits findings into confirmed and needs-verification at a confidence of 65, and the notes carry 100 and 95, so they land on the confirmed side. The cover above says the result is incomplete, so the page is honest about the scan, while the list under it reads as if two vulnerabilities were confirmed. The three changes:

  • The scan’s own notes move out of the findings. The owner’s page, the share page, the print layout, the PDF export and the Markdown copy list them under “About this scan.” A scan with notes and no findings says “No findings were reported” and points at the notes, where it used to count them as confirmed findings. The category filters no longer include the notes, and the “confirmed” bars count findings only.
  • An active-test finding lists its requests. The panel reads Endpoint: and Request: lines as well as GET /path lines, and says “This finding’s evidence lists no request lines” when it finds none. Endpoint: counts for active tests only, because on a passive finding it may only say where something was seen.
  • The ledger keeps up to 500 finding names per test, up from 40. A test that raises more still records its true count. Saved reports keep the names they have, and new scans carry the full list.

Why it earns the headline

Appendix A is a list of times a report said something false or claimed more than anyone had checked. A person holding the raw output and the code found each one. A report that shows its work moves some of that checking to the reader. The audit’s own rule points the same way: “An evidence string is a claim that can be checked.” Showing the work extends that rule from one line of evidence to the whole report, and the sections on how a scanner lies and on live apps show what getting there took.

The first real report is a small case of it. The reader of that PDF could see what was skipped and why, and could see an OWASP flag that the report’s own text contradicted. The fix session saw both, PR 16 was open two minutes after the upload, and it merged at 11:03 UTC. That loop, a report that can be argued with and a fix that follows, is the working form of the claim. Whether the fixes hold on a live report is the part that is still open.

On the fixture app, “sensitive file exposure” raised 78 findings and kept 40 names, so 38 of the 199 findings have no check on record. All 38 are exposed-file names. Their “How this was found” text says “Which check raised this was not recorded for this report.” The first Critical on the fixture’s screen is one of them (Figure 5). The cap is one line in testLedger.ts. Reran A real site seldom raises 78 findings from one test, so I expect this to show mostly on the fixture. I have not seen them on a real scan, and the TLS reason has appeared on no screen. I rendered draft PR 17’s branch the same way, on stand-ins only.   • The proof cases were written with the fix. The seven stand-ins come from the session that wrote PR 14. They show that the fix does what its author meant on the cases its author imagined. The two real reports are scans of two sites, both graded A. Whether real apps behind real platforms look like the stand-ins is the open question in the next section.

Wording for the claim

Supported: “Every SecScan report lists the tests it ran and the ones it skipped, with the reason, and says when it could not see your app.” A real report shows the first part. Supported on stand-in screens: “shows how each finding was found.” The panel is on the owner’s screen only. The PDF I read from the real site has the evidence and the fix and no panel. Unsupported: “No other scanner does this.” The research found only that no rival advertised a per-scan ledger, and it did not compare reports. The earlier advice stands for the other words: never say pentest, certified, compliant or false-positive free.

What would settle it

Choose one behind a platform gate or one built on a platform such as Replit, Lovable or Bolt if there is one, hand-check the output and compare it with what Carlos saw on October 1. The seclayer.app scan answers whether a healthy app gets a sane report. Only a scan that a platform page answers shows whether the gate holds. The fix session lists the same step first. It needs the app addresses or the report links, and a fresh sweep of the thirty sites needs a machine that can reach them.

The method

A quiet scanner proves nothing

Scanning a well-run website and finding almost nothing is the correct result. It is also the result a broken scanner gives. The project’s own validation notes put it plainly.

A scanner that reports nothing has a perfect false-positive rate.

DETECTION-VALIDATION.md, Public eyes folder

A scanner can fail in two directions. It can report what is not there, which is a false positive. It can miss what is there, which is a false negative. Each direction needs its own kind of target. A well-run site has a known right answer of few findings and no false ones. A deliberately vulnerable app has a known right answer of every planted fault. The project uses both, and adds hand checks, a blind comparison against two other scanners, a code review of every probe and a large automated test suite.

InstrumentThe question it answersWhat it cannot tell you
Planted-flaw check (19 faults)
Does the scanner still find the basics? It exits non-zero on a miss, so it can gate a build.
Anything beyond its 19 faults.
Fixture gate (88 faults)
Does the full scanner, in active mode with two accounts, find every fault in the test app and stay quiet on the clean twins?
Anything the checklist lacks, because the app is built from the checklist.
Blind benchmark (74 faults)
How does it compare with OWASP ZAP and Nuclei on the same target, scored by judges who do not know which tool is which?
Superiority. The target favours SecScan, the judges are AI models and ZAP was not fully configured.
Live sweeps of well-run sites
Does it invent problems on sites that are known to be well run?
Whether it detects real problems. Quiet output alone proves nothing.
Hand checks
Is each reported finding true on the live site, using plain requests and DNS lookups?
Anything that was not checked. On Sept 24 only the 16 highs were.
Code review with benign inputs
Which healthy responses would make a probe fire?
What the reviewers did not think of.
Clean-twin hosts (4, October 1)
Does the scanner invent findings on a host with every fault removed, including hosts that answer 200 to anything?
How real customer apps behave. Four hosts, built by one reviewer from one small server.
Stand-in apps (7, October 1)
When a platform’s page, a challenge or an error answers in place of the app, does the scanner say so and keep it out of the grade?
How real apps on those platforms behave. Seven local servers, written by the session that wrote the fix.
Automated tests (2,699 API, 141 frontend)
Does each finding appear when its condition is present and stay silent when it is absent?
How a third-party site behaves on a given day.
Retest baselines
Did a change shift the counts on four known sites?
Whether the counts were right in the first place. Two of its baselines predate the Sept 30 SRI fix.

Instrument one

A test app that is wrong on purpose

To count what a scanner misses, you need a target whose faults you know in advance. The project built one. The vulnerable fixture is an app that plants a real instance of every finding that can be seen over HTTP, running on a local port. It is test infrastructure and is never built into the product image. Every secret in it matches a real vendor’s format closely enough for the detector to fire, and none of them is live.

Three counts for three instruments

InstrumentCountWhat it runsWhen
Planted-flaw check detection-check.ts
19 of 19, returning 34 findings
A quick pass with active probing on. It asks only whether each of 19 planted flaws was found.
Sept 24 Reported
Fixture gate verify-vuln-fixture.ts
80 of 80 on Sept 26, 82 of 82 with 194 findings on Sept 30, and 88 of 88 with 199 findings on merged master
The real scanner, active probing on, two credentialed accounts. Non-zero exit on any miss.
Sept 26 to Oct 1 Reported Reran Oct 1
Benchmark ground truth
74 faults
The same app, scored against ZAP and Nuclei by blind judges.
Sept 22 to 24 Reported

The fixture README used to say 73 tracked findings and 34 secret patterns, which went stale. PR 14 removed the count of findings and the README now says 35 patterns. Verified The gate’s rise from 82 to 88 came with the mass-assignment check on create endpoints and the real-shaped secret plants.

The first score was 18 of 19

The missed fault was an AWS key. The key that had been planted was Amazon’s own documented example key, and the scanner correctly ignores placeholder keys. The test had exercised the false-positive guard instead of detection. A realistic key made the finding appear at once. Both behaviours were right.

The gate that expected a false positive

On September 30 a review found that the fixture’s /app/config.json held only public runtime settings, an API address and a feature flag, and the gate expected the scanner to report it. That expectation was the false positive itself. The scanner now reports a config file only when it carries a credential-shaped key. The planted file gained a dbPassword, and a public-config twin at /uploads/config.json was added that no finding may name. The gate stayed at 82 of 82 with no false alarm. Reported

Every new check ships with a clean twin

The project’s rule for new checks is a vulnerable case and a clean twin in the fixture. A rule that fires on the vulnerable case and stays silent on the twin is the closest thing to a controlled experiment in the repository.

What an app cannot plant

Some checks look outside the application server, so the fixture cannot exercise them. Each one needs real infrastructure, which is a separate decision and not a gap in the app.

  • SPF, DMARC and DNSSEC records need a domain with deliberately broken DNS.
  • Mail transport checks need a real mail server on port 25.
  • Subdomain takeover needs an abandoned cloud resource behind a dangling CNAME.
  • Open-port checks need real listeners, some on privileged ports.
  • Public bucket listings need real cloud storage accounts.
  • Appwrite, PocketBase, Firebase and Supabase checks need real, deliberately misconfigured projects.

Two further limits are on record. The SSRF probe needs a reachable out-of-band collector. And all 78 sensitive paths are served, but the gate asserts only a sample of about ten by name, because checking all 78 individually would make the script the likeliest place for a typo. The same 78 meet a different limit in the report, whose ledger keeps 40 names per test. See Showing the work.

Instrument two

SecScan, ZAP and Nuclei meet the same target

The same vulnerable app, grown to 74 planted faults, was scanned by SecScan, OWASP ZAP and Nuclei. Three separate AI judges decided, without knowing which tool was which, whether each tool’s findings showed detection of each fault. They agreed on 213 of 222 decisions. Every credit traces to raw scanner output. Reported

What SecScan missed

Six of the 74. One is an SSRF case. Five are access-control and API cases: an API with no authentication, function-level access, cross-account access, a page-level IDOR and guessable identifiers. These tests need two logins, an API spec or an out-of-band collector, and the research did not confirm whether this run had all of them configured. The fixture gate, run separately with two accounts, detects the tracked faults.

How the benchmark caught itself

The first blind run scored ZAP at 18 of 74 and Nuclei at 9, against SecScan’s 68. Before publishing, the raw ZAP crawl log was checked against the ground truth. ZAP had never requested /download, /login or /app/graphql. It had not visited and missed them. Nothing on the fixture’s homepage linked to them, while SecScan reached them from a built-in path list. That is SecScan knowing its own test app, and not a detection win.

The fix linked every genuine feature from the navigation, so any ordinary crawler finds them. Deliberately hidden paths such as /admin and /backup stay unlinked, because finding them by forced browsing is a fair and disclosed capability difference. ZAP’s default full scan does not enable its forced-browse add-on, and that asymmetry is disclosed and not corrected.

An earlier problem shaped the scoring. Three rounds of adjusting regular expressions moved ZAP’s score from 59.5% to 47.3% to 31.1% on identical scan data. Hand-written patterns scoring a competitor’s tool cannot be trusted, which is why the scoring moved to blind judges.

A tool scoring lower here has not been shown to be worse. It has been shown to overlap less with SecScan’s checklist.

artifacts/api-server/scripts/benchmark/README.md

Read this before quoting the table

  • The test app was built to contain what SecScan checks for. It measures SecScan’s false negatives well, and it is an inherently favourable test in any comparison.
  • ZAP ran in full-scan mode without its forced-browse wordlist, its API-spec import or logins. Its scores on hidden paths and access control mean “not configured for it.”
  • The matching is deliberately generous to the other tools. Where a tool reports something broader than the planted fault, it is credited. The report also prints what each tool found that was not planted.
  • The judges are AI models and share whatever blind spots such models have. Nobody outside the project has reproduced the result.
  • The benchmark output folder is listed in .gitignore, so the raw outputs and judge verdicts are not in the repository. Publishing them would turn this from the project’s number into one others can re-score. Verified
  • None of the vibe-app scanners, SecScan’s closest rivals, were in the head-to-head.

Instrument three

Thirty well-run sites, three times

The corpus is thirty well-known sites across six sectors, first scanned on September 8 and again on September 24 and September 30, plus 20 guard targets built into the live-scan script. Scans are passive. They send HTTP GETs and DNS lookups against publicly served pages, attempt no login, manipulate no parameters and change nothing on any site. On sites like these a correct scan returns few findings and no false ones, so every actionable finding is checked against the live response.

September 24: the first published sweep

The sweep returned 282 findings across 30 sites, 98 of them above Info: no critical, 16 high, 44 medium, 38 low and 184 info, from 299 pages fetched. Eight sites answered with a bot-protection page and were withheld. On the 22 sites that were reached the grades were A for 3, B for 9, C for 9 and D for 1, with a mean score of 22.6. Verified The numbers reproduce exactly from the raw output.

All 16 highs were checked by hand that day, with a browser user agent, a plain one and DNS lookups. Fifteen were confirmed and one carried a note.

High findingSitesWhat the check found
Missing Content-Security-Policy
europa.eu, fastly, gitlab, nasa, shopify, slack, wikipedia, zoom
HTTP 200 on both requests and no policy header. (gitlab.com was later shown to set its policy in a meta tag.)
Policy missing on internal routes
bbc (3), cloudflare (9), github (1), vercel (8)
The root sends a policy and the re-fetched routes return 200 with none. GitHub’s is /healthz, which answers as HTML.
JavaScript source map exposed
fastly, gitlab, archive.org
HTTP 200 with 126, 301 and 3 source files. archive.org’s is a vendored copy of a public library, so High was arguably too severe.
Missing DMARC record

The domain and its parent both answer NXDOMAIN, while the parent publishes real MX records.

The false positive on amazon.co.uk

The first run reported “Missing Content-Security-Policy” at High, plus four smaller header findings, for amazon.co.uk. The hand check showed that Amazon does not serve its homepage to this kind of request. It serves either a 2 KB Akamai bot-manager page that runs a proof-of-work script, or a 4 KB “click the button below to continue shopping” robot check. The scanner’s challenge detector recognised neither, so it read an interstitial as Amazon’s homepage. All five findings described a page Amazon never published.

Both pages are now recognised by fingerprints only they carry, with five regression tests, two of which protect a real page that merely mentions the same words. A second bug surfaced in the same result. Akamai’s edge server identifies itself as AkamaiGHost and a pattern matched “ghost,” labelling the site as the Ghost blogging platform. The technology list feeds the CVE monitor, so every Akamai-fronted site would have been sent Ghost advisories. It now matches on a word boundary.

September 30: the re-sweep

The September 30 round re-ran the same 30 sites and the 20 guard targets, then checked every difference from September 24 against the live response using the scanner’s own user agent. It re-derived the header findings independently (policy, nosniff, clickjacking, base-uri, cookies, HTTP redirect) and checked source maps, DMARC and internal-route findings by hand. The audit counts actionable findings falling from 98 to 92 on the first run. After the fixes it ran a second sweep.

On the 22 sites that were graded both times, the comparison below is recomputed from the committed raw files. Thirteen actionable findings left the list and seven entered it. Highs fell from 16 to 14 and actionable findings from 97 to 91. The mean score moved from 22.6 to 20.0, and the D grade is gone. Verified

Seven kinds of wrong finding

Every row below was present in the September 24 output and every one is fixed, with a test that fails on the old code.

ReportedSitesWhy it was wrong
Weak CSP (Medium)
archive.org, bbc.co.uk
archive.org’s script-src holds only origins and 'wasm-unsafe-eval'. On bbc.co.uk 'unsafe-inline' sits beside a nonce and 'strict-dynamic', so browsers ignore it.

The header is sent twice, and the old exact match read it as invalid.

The scripts are the site’s own subdomain or CDN. Dropbox’s one real third-party script carries integrity.

The records have 9 and 10 lookups. IPv6 ranges were being counted.
Non-session cookie without Secure

Permissive CORS (Medium)

ACAO: * with no credentials. Now Info.

The seventh kind is the one that follows from checking source maps by whose code they hold. Source-map severity now depends on what the map embeds. archive.org went from High to Low. fastly.com now shows both of its maps, the library one at Low and a second one that holds the site’s own component at High. The first run had reported only the first map it found. Reported

Not everything moved down

Several findings went up or appeared. gitlab.com’s High for a missing policy disappeared because the policy is delivered in a meta tag. Reading it exposed two real Mediums, an unsafe-inline and unsafe-eval policy in script-src and a permissive object-src. npmjs.com answered with its real page on one run, and four findings on it were confirmed by hand. apnews.com did the same on the re-sweep and its seven findings matched an independent fetch.

Withheld on purpose

Whether a site answers the scanner with a bot challenge changes from run to run. Eight sites did on Sept 24, seven on the first Sept 30 run and six after the fixes. When an edge answers instead of the origin, every content-derived check describes the interstitial. The scanner detects that, reports it once as a coverage note and withholds those findings. DNS, email-authentication and mail-transport findings stay, because they never read the intercepted response. Etsy’s report went from 18 findings to 4 under this rule. A withheld site is suppressed coverage and not a clean result, and its counts are not comparable with the rest.

What these sweeps describe

They describe the scanner as it stood on September 30, at 5d19cad. PR 12 to 14 have since changed ratings and signatures. A session cookie without SameSite is now Low. Language and preference cookies no longer draw a “readable by JavaScript” finding. The jQuery, Lodash, Alpine, HTMX and Google Analytics tags need a script path or a library-only call. Certificates of 100 days or less warn at 14 and 7 days only. The GitHub Pages and Rails tags need real markers. The tables in Appendix B were not re-run, and a fresh sweep needs a machine that can reach the sites. Verified In the changelog and the diff.

A note on the sites named here

Grades and findings on third-party sites are SecScan’s output from passive reads of public pages. They show how the scanner behaves. They are not assessments of those organisations’ security, and several of the Sept 24 findings were later shown to be wrong.

Failure modes

How a scanner lies

On September 8 the scanner told its readers that the UK government’s own website had no SPF record and no DMARC policy, and it rated both High. gov.uk publishes v=spf1 -all and p=reject, the strictest answers a domain can give. The audit that recorded the mistake called it the most email-secure domain a UK scan is likely to meet.

Three bugs stacked up behind that one finding. The code guessed the email domain by counting letters, took gov.uk for a .co.uk-style name and looked in the wrong place. A mail lookup returned two CNAME records and the code counted them as mail servers, which raised the severity. The evidence line said “domain exists” whatever the resolver had answered, and for the name it had asked about the answer was NXDOMAIN.

Reading the presence of a response as the meaning of the response.

FALSE-POSITIVE-AUDIT.md, September 8, naming an error it had by then recorded four times

Since September 7 the project’s records list 66 defects of this kind. An entry here is a wrong finding, a right finding with wrong evidence, or a report that claimed more than anyone had checked. Sorted by cause, six habits account for 61 of them, and the other 5 are oddities.

Presence read as meaning

Something arrived, so the scanner took it for an answer. A mail server reset the connection after the handshake and the scanner concluded that it offered no encryption. A bot filter set a header on traffic it had allowed and the scanner concluded the traffic was blocked. A CVE alert went to every nginx site because a CVE’s prose mentioned nginx. In three real hours of vulnerability-database data one CVE did, and none affected it.

The mail-server case had a second problem. It fired on some runs and not on others, depending on when the reset landed. The audit’s verdict is that this is worse than a consistent false positive, because whoever disputes the report cannot reproduce it, and a re-run makes it vanish.

Loose parsing

A rule accepted text it should have refused. Administratoren contains /admin/i, so a Wikipedia robots file was said to disclose an admin path. AkamaiGHost contains “ghost,” so Akamai sites were tagged as the Ghost blogging platform. A wildcard check fired on https://*.onetrust.com. A comma inside a cookie’s expires date split the cookie in half and hid the flags after it. The fixes share a shape. Parse the thing, match whole words, and stop searching for a pattern inside a string that has structure.

A stand-in for the target

The scan describes a page the site never published. Amazon answered the scanner with a 2 KB bot-manager page that runs a proof-of-work script, or a 4 KB robot check, and the scanner took it for Amazon’s homepage. The result was a High and four smaller findings about a page Amazon never served. Twelve of the 18 findings on Etsy had the same cause. When an edge answers instead of the origin, every check that reads content describes the answer.

The project’s defence is to recognise the interstitial, withhold those findings and say so. It worked until a host answered 200 to everything, which is the subject of Hosts that say yes. October 1 added three more stand-ins of the same shape, a sign-in wall, a stopped deployment and a challenge that only the browser saw. The section on live apps covers them.

The October 1 reruns found the same shape inside the report’s own coverage list. After PR 14, a scan that a wall had answered withheld its findings and still listed 18 of its 40 tests as ran, two of them with finding counts for findings it had just withheld. PR 15, which merged at 10:38 UTC, marks those tests as not tested on the app. Reran

An unobservable claim

A single GET to a homepage cannot see rate limiting. Stripe sends no rate-limit headers and certainly limits rates. The check had been patched twice, once for Google’s server token and once for GitHub’s edge, which the audit describes as a check chasing an unobservable property one vendor at a time. It fired on 15 of 30 sites. It is now an Info note that says only that rate limiting is not advertised.

Evidence that argues against the finding

PayPal showed the subtlest case. The scan had correctly found that internal pages lacked frame-ancestors, but the evidence printed each address without its query string. The linked address, /giving?locale.x=en_US, answers with one policy. The bare /giving answers with a different one, and that one has the directive. Anyone who verified the way the audit tells reviewers to verify would fetch the printed address, find the header present and decide the scanner was broken.

The audit’s own rule

“An evidence string is a claim that can be checked. If it points somewhere the scanner did not look, it does not merely fail to support the finding, it argues against it.” The audit adds that this was the one defect in its pages that would have caused a correct check to be deleted.

One look, or flaky

reddit’s edge sends its CSP header on some responses and not on others, for the same path, seconds apart. The finding was real, but a gap seen once cannot be reproduced by the person who disputes it. The scanner now looks a second time and keeps only gaps that are still there. nasa.gov’s DNS lookup returns SERVFAIL about one time in ten, and the scanner read that error as “no SPF record” on one scan in five. Ten of ten scans were clean after the fix.

Something else

Three entries fit no habit. One cookie was reported twice. A results script printed “every actionable finding here was verified by hand” on every run, whether or not anyone had looked. And inner-page cookie findings quoted live cookie values in their evidence. Reports are stored, emailed as PDFs and readable through share links, so on a signed-in scan the value was a working session token. Nothing in the repository redacted it, and the committed raw files had been cleaned by hand.

The quiet half

Every defect above makes the scanner say something false. The mirror image makes it stay silent about something true, and that is harder to notice. On September 19 the audit recorded that more than a dozen probe families were wrapped so that a crash returned an empty list. A check that blew up looked the same as a check that ran and found nothing. A real finding, archive.org’s missing HTTPS redirect, had simply been absent from a full scan with no trace. The next day every family became tracked, and a failure now shows up as an Info note naming the check groups that could not be completed.

On October 1 the same shape turned up in the browser step, which Hosts that say yes describes. A third source of silence is deliberate. The September 30 review narrowed several checks so they stop firing on healthy sites, and the audit says plainly that a real problem in those shapes can now be missed.

How the ledger was built

Each row comes from the audit, a commit message, one of the October 1 reports or my own reruns, and the full list is in Appendix A. The seven causes are my grouping. Where a defect had two causes I used the one the audit names first. Reran for the 13 rows I reproduced on October 1: the six clean-host rows, the stand-in rows, the test ledger rows and the withheld-scan row. Reported for the other 53. The 14 findings from the September 24 output that the September 30 round showed to be wrong or over-rated, on 12 of the 30 sites, are recounted from the raw JSON.

September 30

Six reviewers, one question

On September 30 six reviewers each took a family of checks and asked what healthy response would make it fire. They fed the real functions realistic, benign responses through a mocked network. That is the opposite of a vulnerable test app. A vulnerable app asks whether the scanner finds what is there. This asked whether it invents what is not.

Every item was reproduced before it was fixed. Every fix has a clean-twin test that failed on the old code, plus a second test showing that the real problem is still found. The fixture gate stayed at 82 of 82 with no false alarms. The review was not a live sweep, so it could only find shapes that somebody thought of. The audit lists 20 fixes across 18 areas. Reported

AreaA benign input that produced a findingNow

Narrowed on purpose

Fixing a false positive usually means making a check stricter, and a stricter check misses more. The audit names four places where that is the trade. In each of them a real problem can now go unreported.

  • An app that renders the same record for any id, including a made-up one, no longer draws an access-control or anonymous-read finding.
  • An unauthenticated DELETE that answers 404 for a missing id is no longer reported. Only success-style replies count.
  • An inner-route .env mixed with lines that are not KEY=VALUE, a config.json without credential-shaped keys and a debug log with fewer than two log-shaped lines are missed.
  • A bucket whose first 100 objects are all static assets reads as Info even if a sensitive file sits further in.

October 1

Hosts that say yes

On the morning of October 1 the project’s own gate was green. All 82 planted faults were found, and every one of the 194 findings on the vulnerable app mapped to a planted fault or to something true about it. A reviewer then asked the question the gate cannot ask. What does the scanner say about an app that has no faults?

They built a clean twin of the test app. It has the same routes, the same login and the same pages, each done safely: strict security headers, real sessions, a CORS policy that names its one allowed origin, escaped output and a rate-limit header on every reply. Four copies of the twin differ in one way only, which is how they answer a path nobody routed. One sends a real 404. One sends the single-page app shell with a 200, as many hosted single-page apps do. One sends a friendly “Page not found” page with a 200. One sends a JSON error with a 200. A fifth run served the shell with a fixed nonce, to rule out the per-request nonce as the trigger, and drew the same findings as the first shell run.

The scanner ran against each in active mode with two signed-in accounts and race testing on. Verified The counts below reproduce from the raw output files, and the rule behind each wrong finding was read in the code. The gate’s 82 of 82 and 194 findings are in the run log in the shared folder. The reviewer’s mapping of all 194 is their own account. Reported

On master the host that sends real 404s drew four findings and all four are true: it is served over plain HTTP, it sets a language cookie that script can read, it has no Twitter card tags and it publishes an OpenAPI file. The same four appear on every copy. The three hosts that answer yes drew two to five more, and none of those is true. These are the “Before” bars in the figure. Reran My runs on master reproduce the reviewer’s raw output finding for finding.

One of the false findings is a Critical, “Write Endpoints Reachable Without Authentication.” Thirty points is enough to turn a C into a D. On the JSON host five false findings added 51 points and the grade fell to F. On the merged code every host scores 30, a C, from the plain-HTTP Critical alone.

Five wrong findings, one cause

Every false finding came from a host that answered 200 to something it never routed. The host with real 404s produced none.

ReportedWhereWhat happened
Write endpoints reachable without authenticationCritical
Shell, soft 404, JSON
The scan sent DELETE to an invoice address and got a correct 401, so it moved on to PATCH. No such route exists. The catch-all answered 200 with the app shell or its “not found” JSON, and the rule counted any 2xx reply as proof that a handler ran. Nothing compared the reply with the catch-all or looked for a “not found” body. isHandlerReached in apiProbeEndpoint.ts.
No rate limiting observed on sensitive endpointsInfo
Shell, soft 404, JSON
A burst of 12 GET requests to /api/me/password, a path the page only ever calls with POST. The catch-all answered 200 twelve times. Every reply also carried RateLimit-Limit and RateLimit-Remaining headers, which this check ignores.
API endpoints served without authenticationHigh
JSON only
GET /api/me/password returned {"error":"not found","path":…,"status":404} with HTTP 200, signed in and signed out. The keys matched, so the check read it as an API open to anyone. A body that says “not found” was never treated as a non-answer. An HTML shell did not trigger it, with or without a nonce.
WordPress XML-RPC enabledMedium
JSON only
The catch-all echoes the requested path, so the body contained the word xmlrpc and passed the validator. The catch-all filter compares body length within 3 percent, and a body that echoes the path changes length with every path.
VS Code workspace settings exposedLow
JSON only
The same mechanism. That validator accepts any JSON longer than 20 bytes.

The shell and the soft 404 page tripped no file rule, because the catch-all check also compares page titles and theirs matched. The JSON host has no title, which is why only it drew the last two findings.

What stayed quiet

The twin carries bait for the scanner’s other false-alarm families. None of it produced a finding: a Stripe publishable key, a Sentry DSN, a Supabase anon token, a form config with type: "password", interface strings named password and api_key_label, an SRI hash and a git SHA. Escaped reflection on /search and /hello stayed quiet, as did page text containing SQLITE_ERROR and You have an error in your SQL syntax, a safe ?next= redirect, an origin-allowlisted CORS policy and a docs page quoting .env, id_rsa and an alg:none JWT. Verified The raw findings hold none of them.

The twin does have one piece of true noise. Every copy reports an Info finding for a lang=en preference cookie that script can read. It is accurate and not worth a reader’s attention.

Why the gate did not see it

The gate is the project’s main regression check, and it does not include a host that says yes. The vulnerable app answers an unknown path with a 500 that carries a debugger signature, and the message on the latest fixture commit says so. The one condition behind every false finding here is a condition the gate does not create. Its clean twins sit inside the checklist and share the checklist’s blind spots. The method section made the same point about the blind benchmark. Reported

The silent loss

The most serious result was a missing finding. When a page looks like a single-page app, the scanner swaps the fetched HTML for the headless browser’s render of it, and until now it never looked at the status of that render. In the reviewer’s container the browser was routed through a proxy, got a 405 error page for 127.0.0.1, and the scanner analysed that page as the site. Of the 82 tracked findings, 36 vanished: every JavaScript secret, the Next.js data, the JWTs, the crawl, injection, IDOR, deserialization, source maps and the AI checks. No coverage note appeared. Reported The code lines are Verified.

That was a container accident, and it exposed a real path. In production the same swap happens whenever the headless browser is answered differently from the plain fetch, for example by a bot challenge served only to headless Chrome. It is the quiet half of the ledger again. The scanner said nothing, and nothing looked the same as clean. The fix session later found that the browser was in fact answered differently, because it sent another name from the plain requests. When the scanner is not looking at the app tells that part.

A right finding at the wrong address

The reflected-XSS finding on the vulnerable app named /?q=, which reflects nothing. The bug is at /search?q=. The evidence line printed the scan’s start path instead of the path that reflected. A customer who tried the printed address would conclude the scanner had cried wolf. The same mistake blinded the gate’s clean-twin check for XSS, which searches the evidence for clean paths such as /hello?. Reran The gate’s raw output names /?q= on master and /search?q= on the merged code. The link-by-link probe is the reviewer’s account. Reported

Gaps in the test app itself

The review found four secret patterns with no real-shaped plant. The planted Slack, Supabase service-role and sb_secret_ values were zero-filled, and the scanner correctly drops them as placeholders, so the patterns they exist to exercise went unverified. The Twilio key pattern was never planted, and the self-test script failed 34 of 35. The fixture README said 34 patterns where there are 35. Reported PR 14 planted real-shaped values. I ran the self-test on both trees: master matches 34 of 35 and misses Twilio, and the merged tree reports 35 of 35. Reran The README on master now says 35 patterns. Verified One gap stays. The behavioural rate-limit check is not planted, and a comment in the gate still says that it fires on the fixture. The comment is there. Verified That the check does not fire is the reviewer’s finding. Reported

What the fixes leave alone

  • Mass assignment on a POST that creates something was missed on master, because the privilege-field check filtered out every endpoint that is not read-shaped. PR 14 reads it from the declared contract, and the gate’s case is now found. Reran Outside the read-shaped set only a published spec counts, so on an app that publishes none, a signup route that the scanner saw only in the app’s own front end is still not considered. The code comment says so. Verified
  • SSRF is still unmeasured, because the probe needs a callback host backed by the database.
  • The browser-render rule has unit tests now, in scanner.gate.test.ts. The fix session says they fail on master and pass on the branch, and they pass in my full run. The reviewer’s original trigger, a proxy answering the browser with a 405, has still not been reproduced. Reported
  • The echo fix handles a body that repeats the requested path. A catch-all that stamps something else into its reply, such as a request id, would still change the length. That is my reading of the code and it is untested.

Barely tested in the wild

The new checks have been read in one of the two real scans

Since September 26 the scanner has gained checks that the thirty-site sweeps never exercised. Nine arrived in that day’s build and four probes arrived on September 29. All of them pass the project’s own tests. On October 1 the rows that hold six of the nine ran on a real site for the first time and raised nothing. None has been seen to fire on a real fault. I read the second real scan, secscan.us, for what it reported and not for these rows, and neither scan ran with the PR 18 changes.

For most of them that is by design. Seven of the nine September 26 checks sit in probe families that run only on a domain whose owner has been verified. The scan code says why in a comment above that list: “That is testing, not visiting.” No third-party sweep can reach them. The other two, the AI checks, are passive. They read the page’s own JavaScript, so they ran on every sweep target. None of the nine new check names appears in any of the 128 site results from the six passive runs of September 24 and 30, and neither “Supabase” nor “Firebase” shows up in any site’s technology list. Verified The silence of the passive pair on these sites is the expected result and proves little.

Four probes from September 29

ProbeWhat it doesGuard rails
Automatic second account
Submits the target’s public signup form once, to get the second login that the cross-account test needs.
Off unless the requester ticks “Create one for me” (since September 30, migration 0024). Monitor rescans never opt in. One POST, forms that post to another host are refused, and the report names the account it made.
LLM prompt injection
Asks a site’s own chat endpoint to repeat its system prompt, and compares the reply with a prompt found in the client code.
Skipped, with a stated reason, when no prompt was found. A refusal that restates the role is not counted as a leak.
Race condition
Sends concurrent requests to a one-time action such as redeem or claim and reports when more than one succeeds.
Opt-in, because it acts on the test account. It needs a refused control request, and a generic 403 or 429 is inconclusive.
GitHub source scan
Reads a named public repository for committed secrets. The form field, API and MCP tool arrived on September 30.
Ignores placeholder, too-deep and test-directory files. Says why a repository was not read, so a failed read is not recorded as clean.

An independent code review of these probes on September 29 found the kinds of bugs this report keeps meeting. A login form was accepted as a signup form. The probe could make up to six accounts. A refusal that restated the prompt was reported as a leak, and a 200 refusal was counted as a race success. A scan that read zero repository files was reported as scanned. All were fixed with regression tests built from the review. Reported

The gate’s October 1 log holds, for the first three probes, three clean twins and 11 edge cases, and all pass. One edge case in each of the last two says that with nothing to test, the result must say so and must not read as a clean run. Verified The GitHub probe was checked another way. A public repository with planted fake credentials went through the real worker. The three planted secrets were found, the placeholder and test files were ignored, and no raw secret reached the saved report. Reported

None of the four ran in Carlos’s seclayer.app scan. The GitHub source scan was skipped because no repository was supplied, the prompt-injection probe because no system prompt was found in the client code, the race condition probe because it is opt-in, and the cross-account test, which needs the second account, because it needs sign-ins for two test accounts. The SSRF test, which these four sit beside and which needs a callback host, did run and raised nothing. Reported

What the clean hosts could and could not say

Each October 1 scan of a clean host wrote a ledger of 40 test rows. On master, 35 rows ran and 5 were skipped on every one, with a reason for each: no repository was supplied, no system prompt was found in the client code, no claim-style endpoint was found, no callback host is configured for SSRF, and the cross-account test had nothing to compare. On the merged code 28 ran and 12 were skipped. The same five are skipped for the same reasons, and seven more rows that used to say “ran” now say what they had nothing to test: JWT analysis, Next.js data, Supabase, Supabase and Firebase rules, PocketBase and Appwrite, cloud buckets and an exposed manifest. Reran Three of the four new probes and the SSRF probe therefore had nothing to look at on those hosts. That is the correct behaviour, and it also means those scans cannot say whether the probes behave on a healthy chat or claim endpoint. The vulnerable app’s clean twins are the only evidence on that point. Carlos’s seclayer.app scan skipped those probes for the reasons above and adds none.

What would settle it

Run the active probes on one or two apps the project owns that really have a chat endpoint, a promo or claim route and an open signup, with the owner’s consent, and hand-check every finding. The September 19 round did this for the older probes on two owned domains and found no false positive. Nothing equivalent exists for the September 26 and 29 checks.

The safety net

Tests and CI

On October 1 the automated suite held 2,699 tests in the API server, 2,585 that run anywhere and 114 that need a real database, and 141 in the frontend. The service that runs them on every push gave 29 pushes no runner. They arrived between 05:16 UTC and 23:17 UTC on September 30, and the next push, at 05:40 UTC on October 1, ran normally. The unchecked work included the browser guard, the dependency patches and the six-reviewer fixes. By 08:39 UTC CI had caught up, and the merge of PR 14 passed all three jobs with Chromium installed and the database tests running. The merges of PR 15 at 10:38 UTC and PR 16 at 11:03 UTC did the same. PR 17, which merged later, passed both of its runs.

What CI checks

Every push and pull request installs from a frozen lockfile, typechecks, installs Playwright’s Chromium, runs the workspace tests, runs the 114 database tests against a Postgres 16 service, verifies that the generated check index is current and builds the frontends. Pull requests and master also build both Docker images, web and secscan, and only master publishes them. Verified The Chromium step and the Postgres service arrived with PR 14. The workflow file says that Railway deploys from the same push independently of CI, so a missing or red CI run never stopped a deploy.

Since PR 17’s fifth commit (runs #245 and #246 on October 2), CI runs the fixture gate, which it did not before, and master has run it since the merge. CI still runs no live sweep. That matters here: the gate has already failed CI in runs #256 and #258, and #259 failed too, for a reason that the live-scan session places in the fixture, covered below. A unit test covers each October 1 fix, and nothing end to end covers a host that answers 200 to everything, because the gate has no such host. Verified In the workflow and the gate.

The dead stretch

The 29 dead runs, #188 to #216, spread over 18 hours and ended in 4 to 7 seconds each. Eighteen were pushes to master and 11 were pushes to two other branches. The first of them was the commit that added the browser guard. I opened the job lists of four of them, the first, the last, #204 and #210. None names a runner or a single step, and GitHub holds no logs for them. Verified

I never established the cause. The readiness audit that morning inferred an account-level problem with Actions, most likely billing or a spending limit. That inference fits the symptoms and nothing I could read confirms it. The first run to get a runner used the same workflow file as the dead ones, so the return was not a repository change. No push arrived in the six hours before it, so the record cannot show when the runners came back.

The cost was 18 hours of unreviewed work. The browser guard, the pre-launch copy fixes, the dependency patches, the six-reviewer fixes, 32 file-split commits and the sweep commits all went through with no CI result. The first one for any of it arrived on October 1.

Back, and finding things

The first live run, #217 on PR 12, failed four tests and nothing else. They are the browserGuard.test.ts tests, which launch a real Chromium. The workflow never installed one. The tests arrived with the browser guard, in the commit whose run (#188) never started, so nobody had seen them fail. PR 12 added a step that installs Playwright’s Chromium before the tests. Runs #219 and #220 passed, and #220 passed all three jobs: typecheck, test and build with the install step and the tests inside it, and both Docker images. Verified

PR 13 hit its own failure. Its new “Browser Rendering Was Not Used” coverage note raised the generated check index from 310 to 311 findings, and the stale SCAN_CHECKS.md failed the index step in run #221. The same thing had failed runs #178 and #180 on September 29, each time fixed by regenerating the file in the next commit. The regenerated file passed in runs #223 and #224. Verified

The first edition inferred that master’s next push would fail the same four tests, because its workflow had no Chromium step until one of those PRs merged. PR 14 merged both at 08:39 UTC on October 1 and carried the step, so the inference was never tested. Run #229 on master passed all three jobs: the check index, the build, both Docker images and the database tests described next. Verified

PR 14’s second round added the database tests to CI. The workflow starts a Postgres 16 service, creates four throwaway databases and runs the 114 tests for billing, signup, OAuth, health and the GitHub wiring one file at a time. Until then they were skipped on every CI run. They passed in runs #227, #228 and #229. In #229 they took 19 seconds. Verified

PR 15 started three runs at 10:02 and 10:03 UTC: the same commit on a second branch (#230), a push to the PR branch (#231) and the pull request run (#232). All three of its CI runs passed, the database tests included. The pull request run, #232, also built both Docker images, which the two push runs skip by design. Carlos merged PR 15 at 10:38 UTC, and master’s run #233 passed all three jobs: the test step with Chromium installed, the Postgres test step, the check index, the build and both Docker images. PR 16 started six runs, and Carlos merged it at 11:03 UTC. Its runs passed: #234 and #235 on the first commit, #238 and #239 on the second. Two runs on a head that was replaced, #236 and #237, were cancelled by the newer push. Master’s run #240 for the merge passed all three jobs. Verified

Before launch

Two ways the scanner could hurt someone

Accuracy is only half of what a security scanner owes its users. It also sends attack-shaped requests and runs strangers’ JavaScript, and a mistake there lands on a third party. On September 30 two commits closed holes of that kind. Neither is an accuracy fix, and neither shows up in any sweep. Reported

An ownership check that followed the wrong address

Active probing needs proof that the requester owns the domain. The gate checked the hostname the requester typed, and the probes ran against the address the scan ended up at after redirects. A requester could verify a domain they owned, have it answer with a redirect to somebody else’s site, and aim injection, path-traversal and API tests at the stranger.

Active probing now continues after a redirect only when the final host is the submitted host’s own subdomain or one the requester has verified too. Otherwise the scan stays passive and the report says that the redirect is why. The author checked it with a script and two local hosts. With the second host unverified it received 176 requests and none was attack-shaped. With it verified it received 275 attack-shaped requests.

A browser that went wherever it was sent

The scanner’s headless Chromium followed redirects and ran the target’s JavaScript with no address check. A target could send it, or its script could send it, to the cloud metadata service or an internal host from inside the project’s own network. The customer’s cookie and authorization header also travelled in context-wide headers, so every host the page loaded, such as analytics and CDNs, received them.

A guard now sits in front of every request in both browsers, the page render and the form login. It fetches each request itself, checks every redirect hop, checks WebSockets and adds credentials only to in-scope requests. Four tests drive a real Chromium: a private target is refused, a redirect onto a blocked host is stopped even after an allowed hop, a page script’s fetch is blocked, and the cookie reaches the scanned host and not a redirect target or a third-party resource. The commit records one known limit. The name is resolved once by the check and again by Chromium, so a DNS-rebinding trick can still slip through. Reported These are the four tests that CI could not run until October 1, when PR 12’s Chromium step arrived. It merged inside PR 14, and master’s run #229 passed with it. Verified

Dependencies
30 advisories in production packages, among them SQL identifier escaping in drizzle-orm.
Patched within each package’s own major version. pnpm audit --prod went from 30 to 0.
Deploys
The worker’s own shutdown handler exited at once and beat the 90-second drain, so every redeploy killed scans in flight. Production could also boot healthy without its encryption key and fail on the first sign-up.
The worker drains, then closes the browser. Production now refuses to start without ENCRYPTION_KEY.

Privacy and terms copy did not describe the AI opt-out, the redaction before findings reach the AI provider, the GitHub option, the opt-in test account or Google as a third party. Pricing copy and structured data implied that paid plans were on sale. A free scan said “Payment confirmed.”
Copy rewritten to say what happens. Paid plans and credits are stated as not yet on sale and the structured-data offers removed. The scan form no longer invites scanning any site.

File size
The project’s rule is no file over 300 lines. scanner.ts had reached 1,559 lines, the report page 3,017, the mailer 1,277 and the worker 1,085.
32 commits, each labelled “no behaviour change,” split every oversized file. The first reports typecheck, 2,153 API tests and the fixture gate at 82 of 82.

That much code moved with no CI result behind it, which is the risk the previous section describes. The tests and the gate were run by hand after the first split, and the later full run against a real database passed with 2,575 tests. The rule has slipped since. The verdict

Is it ready?

Not yet, and the distance is shorter than it was in the first edition. On well-run sites the passive checks report no false finding we know of, within the limits set out in the table at the top. The false Critical on the clean test hosts that answer 200 to everything is fixed and merged, and the real report from Carlos’s first scan lists its tests with a reason for each one skipped. Reported What has not happened is a scan of any real app that sits behind a platform page, or a fresh sweep. Behind that sit a set of new checks that have never fired on a real fault, a platform gate that lacks several platforms, two display fixes that no live report has shown yet, three more in a pull request that has merged and not been seen on a live scan, and a few pages of stale copy.

This is my reading of the evidence above, and the decision to launch is Carlos’s. One point deserves a second look from the person who knows the customers. The product is aimed at people who ship apps built with AI tools, and many of those apps live on platforms for which the gate has no signal yet: stopped Replit apps, Netlify’s missing-site page, Fly.io and the placeholder pages of Lovable, Bolt and Base44. I did not measure how common that is. If it is common, the likeliest first complaint is a report about a platform’s page with the app unscanned, which is the symptom the fix session was chasing.
