Unproven
Public claims match the product
The landing page, llms.txt and the README are fixed. The Public eyes folder and the repository’s results file are stale, and “no other scanner does this” is a hypothesis that rests on one day of reading rivals’ pages.
Stale in places
Payments
Off by design until the sweep is accepted. Going live is configuration, not code.
Your decision

The order I would work in

  1. Decide on draft PR 20, which fixes what PR 17 left.

    PR 17 was merged on Carlos’s word. It addresses three gaps the screens showed and, since Carlos chose “Fix totals first,” makes the server’s totals leave the scan notes out. CI passed on all five commits, and no independent review of the code is on record. Reports saved earlier keep their old totals, and no screen has been rendered with the last commit. On October 3 Carlos wrote “fix em all”, and draft PR 20 now covers saved reports, the alert and the buttons. It is not merged, and merging is Carlos’s word. Verified The runs and the state of the pull request.

  2. Rescan seclayer.app once the last build is deployed.

    PR 16 is merged and master’s run #240 passed. I cannot see whether Railway has deployed it. A rescan should show the reason beside the TLS grade B and the grey info note on the OWASP card, which would be the first live sighting of both fixes and of the SSL Labs fields they read. PR 17 has merged, so once it is deployed the rescan is also the first look at it on a real scan. Verified The merge and the run.

  3. Scan more of Carlos’s live apps with the current scanner.

    The first one, seclayer.app, came back clean. Choose the next one behind a platform gate or on a builder platform if there is one, hand-check every finding and compare with what Carlos saw earlier on October 1. This settles whether the four causes explain everything, and it is the first test of the platform signals against real responses. It needs the app addresses or the report links.

  4. Add the missing platform signals and check the fingerprints written from memory.

    Use captured responses from real stopped apps, missing sites and placeholder pages. Then look at the new report screens, the PDF and the print view on real reports.

  5. Run a fresh 30-site and 20-guard sweep from a machine that can reach them.

    Hand-check every actionable finding, as the September rounds did, then regenerate the Public eyes folder and the repository’s results file from it.

  6. Put the clean twins and the fixture gate into CI, and run the browser tests in the scanner image.

    CI already runs the database tests and the browser tests on its runner. The gate would catch a regression without a person remembering to run it, and the image is where production runs the guard.

  7. Prove the new checks on one or two apps the project owns.

    Choose apps with a chat endpoint, a claim route, an open signup and a Supabase or Firebase project, and hand-check each finding. Nothing equivalent exists for the September 26 and 29 checks.

  8. Decide the open questions.

    U12, the brand plan, which deploy guide is true, the severity of “CSP missing on an internal route,” and how to word the transparency claim.

  9. Switch payments on last.

    Restricted Stripe live key and webhook secret, the two Railway variables and a database backup, from the payments guide.

Method and limits

How far to trust this report

This report is mostly a synthesis, with a layer of my own reruns. I wrote it from the project’s documents, its raw scan files, its GitHub record, the work of three review sessions and the fix session on October 1, a PDF of Carlos’s first real scan, the cover of the second and, new in this edition, my own runs of the merged code and of draft PR 17’s branch on local stand-ins. None of my scans touched a real site. That shapes what each number is worth, and the mark beside it says which kind it is.

What I checked myself

  • The Sept 24 and Sept 30 sweep tables, the grade counts, the 22-site comparison and the scores, recomputed from the raw JSON with the documented weights.
  • The October 1 clean-host findings, their scores and the 40-row test ledger of every October 1 local scan, read from the raw files in the shared folder.
  • The eleven skip reasons in Carlos’s PDF, set against the ledger rows of my own runs. They match, wording and all.
  • The text of the report screens I rendered, set against the scan data the browser was given: the counts on the two coverage cards, the 12 withheld findings, the OWASP counts, and the findings list of the sign-in wall scan, which holds two Info notes with confidence 100 and 95. On draft PR 17’s branch I set the counts and the card text against the same data, and the fixture rescan against master’s, finding by finding: the same 199 findings by name, category and severity.
  • The readers of the report summary, by searching the API and the frontend for its totals: the cover, the share page and its description, the print layout, the Markdown copy, the PDF cover, the history of a monitored site, the scan email, the executive summary and the MCP server’s text of a report.
  • The absence of the nine new check names from 128 site results, by searching the raw files.
  • The 239 scans in the repository’s raw files, and the 111 before September 24.
  • The workflow file, the generated check index, the build report, the audit, the roadmap and the retest procedure, read in the repository.
  • The Actions record for runs #165 to #244, including the test totals in the logs of #217, #224 and #242, the last steps of #229, the merge into master, the job and step results of PR 15’s three runs and of master’s runs #233 and #240, the pass or fail of the six runs for PR 16, and the four runs for draft PR 17.
  • The diff of PR 13, and the parts of PR 14, PR 15 and PR 16 that this report describes: the platform gate, the provenance panel, the coverage rewrite, the technology rules, the CI workflow, the OWASP count and the TLS grade note. I also read the diff of draft PR 17, which I wrote. A second session with read-only access then checked this report’s text about the draft against the code and the record, and I checked each point it raised before I changed anything.
  • The count and cause tally of the 66-row accuracy ledger. Each row traces to a line in the audit, a commit message, an October 1 report or one of my reruns.

What I ran myself

These are the items marked Reran. I extracted master after PR 14, master before it, the head of PR 15, whose tree became master at 10:38, and master after PR 16 from git into scratch folders, built them and ran them on my own machine. On every tree after the first edition’s I ran seven stand-in apps, five clean hosts, a challenge stand-in that I wrote for this edition and the fixture gate. On master now I also ran the check index and the API and frontend test suites. The secret self-test and a server that records the browser’s name I ran on master before PR 14 and after it. I ran the database tests on master after PR 14 only. PR 15 and PR 16 touch no browser-launch code, no secret pattern and no database test file, and the Postgres step passed in CI on both merges. I also ran the frontend of master after PR 16 in Chromium on its development server, with the API stubbed in the browser from the saved output of my own scans, for five of them: the fixture, the Vercel sign-in wall, the stopped Railway deployment, the hardened app and a clean twin. For the sign-in wall scan I also opened the share page, the PDF export, the Markdown copy and the print layout. No API server, login or database was involved. On the committed head of draft PR 17 I ran the check index and the API and frontend suites, rescanned the fixture and opened the same screens, the share page, print layout, PDF export, Markdown copy and phone width included, again with the API stubbed. I took the captures and the fixture rescan twice, once from my working tree before the commits were made and once from the head, and the results matched. The inputs, the raw output (the draft’s rescans and test logs included) and the scripts are in audit/report-verification-2026-10-01/ in the shared project folder, with a README that says how to repeat them, and the draft’s captures are in audit/pr17-verification-2026-10-01/. Reran

What I only relayed

  • Every hand check of a live site, from the September audit rounds. The live sites were unreachable from my environment.
  • The benchmark scores and the judges’ agreement, which the project reports and nobody has reproduced.
  • The test counts from commit messages and the readiness audit, and the main test step’s total in run #229.
  • The September 30 six-reviewer findings, and the fix session’s account of how it found the four causes of the October 1 symptoms.
  • What Carlos saw when scanning live apps on October 1, which came to me in a message. The apps and the reports were not recorded. The one exception is the PDF of the seclayer.app scan, which I read and cannot check against the site.
  • The platform signals in the gate, which the fix session says come from the platforms’ documentation.
  • The competitor research, which dates from September 24 and was spot-checked on September 28 for three rivals.

What I did not do

I scanned no real site and ran no sweep. I read Carlos’s first PDF in full and the cover of the second, and did not rescan either domain. The scans, gates and tests above ran on my own machine against local stand-ins, and I have seen no report screen on a real scan. I changed no repository code, configuration or copy, with one exception: draft PR 17, which I wrote and opened on October 1 after Carlos chose “Fix all three,” and which was merged on Carlos’s word at 11:23 UTC on October 2. On October 2, after Carlos chose “Fix totals first,” I pushed a fourth commit to it. Also on October 2 I corrected two sentences of its description: SARIF export already lists notes apart from findings and is not affected by the totals, and the button on a note’s card, which the description called “Verify fix,” reads “Check my fix.” I rewrote the description again with the fourth commit. I merged, approved and reviewed nothing. Besides this report I produced a note on the sweep section, the verification folders for the fix session and for draft PR 17, and an entry in the project’s file notes, all in the shared project folder.

Judgement calls

  • The status labels in the three-asks table, the claims table and the open list are my reading of the evidence. Another reader could grade a row one step higher or lower. The mark beside each statement says how that statement is known.
  • The seven causes in the accuracy ledger are my grouping, and where a defect had two causes I used the one the audit names first. Another reader could sort a few rows differently, though the order of the causes would hold.
  • I counted the plain-HTTP Critical on the clean twins and on the stand-ins as a true finding, because they listen on 127.0.0.1 over HTTP and the twin’s own comment calls it a transport fact. That is why every clean host starts at a C.
  • The seven stand-ins were written by the session that wrote the fix, so each shows that the fix handles the case its author imagined. I wrote the challenge stand-in myself from the fingerprints the scanner documents for a Cloudflare challenge. It shows that the code path works and says nothing about what a real challenge looks like. I used them because nothing else was reachable. The circularity is why the verdict asks for more scans of Carlos’s live apps.
  • PR 14 re-rated a session cookie without SameSite from Medium to Low, one day after the project decided to keep it at Medium. Both calls rest on the same browser behaviour. I report the change and take no side.
  • Draft PR 20, the three PR 17 leftovers, was written by me too, and no independent review of it is on record. Draft PR 17 and the stand-in data behind its screens were written by me, the same session that wrote this report, so no independent review of the fix or of the evidence for it is on record. A screen that matches the code I wrote is the expected result. The marks on those figures say Reran for that reason.
  • Dates follow the audit’s own labels and the GitHub timestamps in UTC. The commits’ local times, in Pacific time, fall on different calendar days for some of the work.
  • The report names 30 third-party sites with SecScan’s passive grades. They show how the scanner behaves, and several of the September 24 findings were later shown to be wrong. Anyone publishing this should decide whether naming those sites is wise.

Appendix F

Every scan and run, one entry each

Carlos asked for every scan written down with what, where, when and why, in explicit detail. This appendix has one entry for each scan, run or read of a report in the audit that I could find in the project folders and records. Each entry says what it was and in which mode, where it ran, when, who ran it, why, what it found, where the evidence is, and what it cannot show. Where a time or a detail was not recorded the entry says “not recorded” and nothing is reconstructed from memory. The mark in the last column is the report’s usual one: Reran means I ran it myself, Verified means I read it in the GitHub record, and Reported means a document or another session says so and I did not repeat it.

The same entries are in a Markdown file, audit/scan-run-inventory-2026-10-02.md. No scan in this appendix was made against a live site since the fixes, except the two reports Carlos supplied in group 6, and those were not rerun.

1. Earlier audit rounds on real public sites, September 7 to 30

These ran on live public sites before this report began. The repository holds 12 raw files with 239 scans, and I have now read the scan counts, scannedAt stamps, withheld counts and finding counts of all 12 myself (entries 1.2, 1.3, 1.5, 1.7, 1.8 and 1.10 to 1.12). For every entry the mode, the reason and the people come from the project’s documents, and I did not see any scan run. Every entry is Reported. None of them is a run of the current build.

7.11
Diagnosis of the fixture-gate miss, and its fix in PR 19 (a draft when diagnosed, merged on October 3, see 5.13).
GitHub job logs and local runs; PR 19 on cc4480/VibeScan-Enterprise-Build
PR 19 was opened at 15:24:21 UTC on October 2 (verified in the GitHub record). Times of the log reading and the local runs not recorded.
The live-scan session.
To find why the gate missed the race check in CI.
The session’s account: the fixture’s page-load script posts to the coupon endpoint, so the scanner’s own headless browser spends the coupon at the start of the scan. The coupon expires after one second, and in local runs the race burst came 1.13 to 1.40 seconds later. On a faster runner the burst lands inside the second, gets five refusals and records that nothing was tested. The fix is fixture only: both coupon calls wait for a click. The session reports 88 of 88 in 10 of 10 local runs on the branch, and 6 of 6 with the page-load call removed and the expiry set to 5 seconds.
PR 19 description; raceConditionProbe.ts line in the log of job 110817971800
I verified the MISSED line in the log of #256, and PR 19’s head 3556ccf, base a913ff3, a draft when I first read it, 1 file, 9 added and 2 removed. I did not read the change or rerun anything. Its CI runs #263 (push) and #264 (pull request run) both passed on 3556ccf, which I read in the GitHub record. That is one clean pair, so the miss is not shown to be gone. The session says it did not compare runner resources, and could not read the early log of the passing run #257, so the cause fits the evidence and is not proved. The session says the 25-run stress in 7.8 passed because local runs were slower than CI. That is its account and it fits the evidence.
Reported
